title: Gumbel Straight Flow: Distilling Autoregressive Models into One-step Flow Maps

paper.title: Gumbel Straight Flow: Distilling Autoregressive Models into One-step Flow Maps
paper.abstract:
Abstract We present Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF), a continuous flow map language model that leverages the noise-data coupling of a pretrained autoregressive language (AR) model.
We theoretically demonstrate that the coupling between Gumbel noise and one-hot token sequences induced by an autoregressive model yields non-intersecting linear paths connecting the noise to the sequence representations.
To further enhance high-quality few-step path sampling, we use a flow map semigroup objective where the tangent (velocity) condition is guided directly by the AR teacher.
Across various benchmarks, including pretraining and downstream tasks, GSF can outperform current few-step language generation baselines.

Model Parallel Generation Deterministic Pairing Straight Path Autoregressive Model ✗ ✓ ✓ Discrete Diffusion Model ✓ ✗ ✗ Continuous Flow (Diffusion) ✓ ✓ ✗ Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF) ✓ ✓ ✓ Autoregressive models (AR) are widely used for language generation due to their strong generative performance. However, their sequential generation process is computationally expensive. To address this limitation, parallel-generation language models based on discrete diffusion or continuous flow models have been introduced ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026a ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, discrete diffusion and continuous-flow models often require many sampling steps to control factorization or discretization errors. To accelerate inference in parallel generative models, a natural direction is distillation, i.e., compressing multi-step iterative generation into a few sampling steps or a single step ( Song et al., 2023 ; Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2025 ; Hayakawa et al., 2025 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2026 ) , often using a discrete diffusion model as a teacher. Given their better empirical performance on text modeling, we explore whether autoregressive (AR) models can be used as more capable teachers. Recent work harnesses AR teachers to supervise parallel student models by constructing deterministic sequence-level noise–data pairs ( Draxler et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . However, learning sequence-level noise-to-data mappings is an exceptionally hard supervised problem; for instance, Gumbel-Distill (GD) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) must still fall back to multi-step refinement over a discrete diffusion backbone. In this paper, we instead define a flow path in one-hot continuous space directly over the AR model’s Gumbel-max sampling. This defines a coupling between the distribution of Gumbel sequences 𝐱 0 {\mathbf{x}}_{0} and corresponding one-hot token vectors 𝐱 1 {\mathbf{x}}_{1} such that, for endpoints distributed according to this coupling, the linear interpolants 𝐱 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝐱 0 + t ​ 𝐱 1 {\mathbf{x}}_{t}=(1-t){\mathbf{x}}_{0}+t{\mathbf{x}}_{1} do not intersect ( Figure 2 ). Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF) then learns these straight paths provided by an AR teacher while enabling parallel generation. Straight paths are desirable: minimizing trajectory curvature allows numerical ODE solvers to generate samples in a few steps without discretization issues ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . We further enhance few-step performance using a flow map parameterization (FMLM) ( Lee et al., 2026 ) where the straight tangent (velocity) supervision is given by the AR teacher. As summarized in Table 1 , GSF is (to our knowledge) the first parallel-generation model to combine deterministic pairing with the straight, non-intersecting trajectory structure of autoregressive sampling. sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: This section introduces Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF), a method for distilling an autoregressive (AR) teacher into a flow map. Section 3.1 analyzes the properties of AR-induced paths (green dotted lines in Figure 3 ), and Section 3.2 explains how to distill these paths into GSF (purple arrow in Figure 3 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Flow Map with AR-induced Gumbel Coupling
sections.text: Figure 5 demonstrates that GSF-FM achieves superior empirical straightness ( Figure 5(b) ), thereby boosting generative performance ( Figure 5(c) ) particularly in the low-NFE regime. However, a substantial gap still persists between its few-step and many-step performance. This motivates us to adopt a flow map parameterization. sections.heading: AR-induced Gumbel coupling produces straighter empirical paths and accelerates flow.
sections.text: We first validate the flow matching formulation on unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on OpenWebText (OWT) ( Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019 ) under a Gaussianized prior ( Figure 5 ). GSF-FM achieves better loss convergence during training ( Figure 5(a) ) due to the coupling. To evaluate the straightness, Figure 5(b) measures a rescaled version of S ⁡ ( { 𝐱 t θ } ) S(\{{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{\theta}\}) along generated trajectories: since a straight path implies the denoiser constantly targets the generated endpoint 𝐱 1 {\mathbf{x}}_{1} , we evaluate the straightness error in cross-entropy scale via CE ( 𝐱 1 ∥ D θ ( 𝐱 t , t ) ) \mathrm{CE}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}\,\|\,D_{\theta}({\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)) . This results in superior generative performance in the few-step regime as measured by the Gradient Moment (GM) score ( Hoogeboom et al., 2026 ) , which evaluates the difference between expected parameter gradients on generated versus real data samples judged by GPT-2 Large ( Figure 5(c) ).

sections.heading: Few-step distillation performance on OpenWebText.
sections.text: Next, we evaluate few-step sampling using the flow map objective across 1, 2, and 4 sampling steps ( Table 4 ). At NFE = 1 \text{NFE}=1 , GSF achieves 114.9 generative perplexity and a gradient moment score of 0.94, outperforming prior distillation models in this step regime. Whereas discrete diffusion distillation baselines collapse at single-step sampling (SDTT: 1260.8; DCD: 5743.2; Di4C (Duo): 370.5), GSF preserves reasonable performance. We also maintain an edge over FMLM variants (FMLM: 168.3; FMLM-re: 140.0). GSF’s GM score decreases monotonically with additional sampling steps, and regarding training speed, Figure 8(b) shows that one-step GM converges faster and improves steadily over the course of training. We can examine the effect of straight continuous-path supervision by comparing GSF with GD, since GD also uses Gumbel noise. However, GD uses a discrete diffusion backbone and does not explicitly exploit path information, resulting in limited performance (PPL: 1475.9) compared with GSF. This may be because directly learning the mapping from Gumbel noise to data is an extremely difficult supervised problem. In contrast, the continuous straight path can provide useful intermediate supervision that helps the model learn this mapping more effectively. Furthermore, as shown in Figure 6 , GSF establishes a favorable Pareto trade-off between perplexity and unigram entropy at 4 sampling steps. Also, Figure 8(c) shows that generative performance improves with model size (from Small: 168M to Medium: 419M), where the Medium student is distilled from a correspondingly larger and stronger AR teacher. We also report LLM-as-a-judge pairwise win rates evaluated by Gemini 3.6-Flash in Figure 7 (with prompt in Appendix G ). Across sampling steps, GSF outperforms FMLM and GD, where 1-step GSF is preferred in over 91% of comparisons even against 4-step GD. Appendix H shows examples of samples of GSF, FMLM, GD, and the corresponding judgment. Similar results are also obtained on the LM1B dataset ( Chelba et al., 2013 ) ( Table 4 ) and on the TinyStories dataset ( Eldan and Li, 2023 ) ( Table 4 ). For the latter, GSF reaches 41.22 PPL at NFE = 8 {\text{NFE}=8} , outperforming few-step flow map baselines (FMLM+: 65.89; FMLM-re: 102.89) as well as continuous flow models integrated over 128 steps (CANDI: 46.32; FLM: 57.50).

sections.heading: Prefix completion on OpenWebText.
sections.text: We evaluate conditional text completion. Models are conditioned on a fixed prefix consisting of the first 50 tokens extracted from held-out OpenWebText sequences and tasked with generating the continuation up to a total sequence length of 100. During sampling, the prefix positions are clamped to their true one-hot representations at each step, while the model generates the continuation tokens in parallel. Results are shown in Table 6 . At NFE = 1 \text{NFE}=1 , GSF achieves a conditional perplexity of 97.9 and token entropy of 4.00, improving upon continuous flow baselines (FMLM: 141.6; FMLM-re: 115.0) and outperforming discrete diffusion distillation methods (SDTT: 374.7; Di4C (MDLM): 376.8; DCD: 703.1). With 2 and 4 sampling steps, GSF scales to 77.5 and 71.4 PPL, whereas FMLM-re plateaus near 99.3. Throughout, GSF maintains stable token entropy ( ≈ 4.0 \approx 4.0 ), showing that the learned conditional trajectories follow the prompt context without degenerate repetition. sections.heading: Abstractive summarization on XSum.
sections.text: We next evaluate task-specific sequence-to-sequence generation on the BBC XSum abstractive summarization benchmark ( Narayan et al., 2018 ) , following the protocol of Hu et al. At NFE = 1 \text{NFE}=1 , GSF achieves 29.5 / 9.1 / 23.4 ROUGE-1/2/L, outperforming the single-step continuous flow baseline ELF (23.0 / 5.5 / 18.9). Remarkably, a single forward pass of GSF ( NFE = 1 \text{NFE}=1 ) already surpasses multi-step diffusion models requiring dozens to thousands of iterations, such as E2D2 (28.4 / 8.3 / 22.0 at ≈ 64 \approx 64 steps) and SeqDiffu (19.3 / 1.7 / 14.1 at 2000 steps). sections.heading: Prior distribution and noise scheduling.
sections.text: We investigate the impact of prior choice and time reparameterization for single-step generation on OpenWebText ( Table 8 ). Using the raw Standard Gumbel prior yields poor gradient moment score ( GM = 1.76 \text{GM}=1.76 , PPL = 133.5 \text{PPL}=133.5 ), which we hypothesize is due to the strong right skew of extreme-value distributions ( Figure 4(a) ). Transforming the prior to a standard Gaussian via Proposition 2 substantially improves GM ( GM = 1.05 \text{GM}=1.05 under linear scheduling). Next, we compare noise schedules: while standard DER parameterization achieves 113.8 PPL, it incurs a higher GM score (1.26) and lower token entropy (4.84). Our Coupled DER schedule ( Figure 4(b) ) obtains the best overall balance: GM = 0.94 \text{GM}=0.94 , PPL = 114.9 \text{PPL}=114.9 , and Ent = 5.07 \text{Ent}=5.07 .

sections.heading: Training and architectural configurations.
sections.text: Table 8 examines the impact of student architecture and training configurations for 1-step generation on OpenWebText: (i) Attention masking : Replacing bidirectional self-attention with causal masking drastically degrades performance ( PPL = 211.0 \text{PPL}=211.0 , GM = 1.62 \text{GM}=1.62 ). While the causal dependencies are enough to model straight trajectories defined by the autoregressive teacher, parallel non-autoregressive generation benefits from bidirectional context: the teacher’s Gumbel coupling provides sequence-level target supervision, but bidirectional self-attention enables the student to coordinate across all tokens simultaneously. (ii) Teacher weight initialization : Training a randomly initialized student increases perplexity from 114.9 to 145.4, showing that transferring pretrained AR teacher representations provides an effective initialization for flow map distillation. (iii) Semigroup loss coupling : While GSF by default optimizes the off-diagonal semigroup loss using random intermediate pairs ( PPL = 114.9 \text{PPL}=114.9 ), restricting the off-diagonal transitions strictly along teacher-coupled paths ( Coupled off-diag. ) further lowers perplexity to 108.4 and GM to 0.89, with a slight decrease in token entropy (5.01 vs 5.07). (iv) Denoiser output parameterization : Predicting logits instead of one-hot targets is slightly worse on both headline metrics ( GM = 0.99 \text{GM}=0.99 , PPL = 125.7 \text{PPL}=125.7 ), supporting the one-hot formulation used throughout. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF), demonstrating that autoregressive models naturally provide optimal, straight trajectories between continuous noise and discrete data tokens. By supervising flow maps along these non-intersecting paths, GSF improves few-step parallel generation across unconditional and conditional benchmarks, offering a promising framework for distilling autoregressive models into fast parallel samplers. In Appendix D we discuss several limitations.

sections.heading: A.4 An Optimal Transport Interpretation of Gumbel Straight Flow
sections.text: We can understand the straightness and non-intersection properties of GSF by reformulating it as a (semi-discrete) optimal transport (OT) problem ( Peyré and Cuturi, 2019 , chapter 5) . In a standard flow matching context where the noise distribution p 0 ​ ( 𝐱 0 ) = p noise ​ ( 𝐱 0 ) p_{0}({\mathbf{x}}_{0})=p_{\text{noise}}({\mathbf{x}}_{0}) and data distribution p 1 ​ ( 𝐱 1 ) = p data ​ ( 𝐱 1 ) p_{1}({\mathbf{x}}_{1})=p_{\text{data}}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}) are both distributions with densities in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , we typically couple/pair the noise and samples independently; this leads to a generative ODE with curved paths. To obtain straight paths, one can couple the noise and data distributions using the joint distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 , 𝐱 1 ) p({\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{1}) with marginals p noise ​ ( 𝐱 0 ) p_{\text{noise}}({\mathbf{x}}_{0}) and p data ​ ( 𝐱 1 ) p_{\text{data}}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}) minimizing 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝐱 0 − 𝐱 1 ‖ 2 ] \mathbb{E}[||{\mathbf{x}}_{0}-{\mathbf{x}}_{1}||^{2}] ( McCann, 1997 ) . This is an optimal transport problem whose solution is of the form p OT ​ ( 𝐱 0 , 𝐱 1 ) = p noise ​ ( 𝐱 0 ) ​ δ T OT ​ ( 𝐱 0 ) ​ ( 𝐱 1 ) p_{\text{OT}}({\mathbf{x}}_{0},{\mathbf{x}}_{1})=p_{\text{noise}}({\mathbf{x}}_{0})\delta_{T_{\textup{OT}}({\mathbf{x}}_{0})}({\mathbf{x}}_{1}) where T OT ​ ( ⋅ ) T_{\textup{OT}}(\cdot) is the optimal transport map. Computing this joint distribution is typically intractable and requires approximations; see e.g. ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . We are here in a specific scenario where the data distribution is an atomic distribution. Again one can obtain straight transport paths if we could identify the joint distribution minimizing the expected quadratic cost. This is a so-called semi-discrete optimal transport problem ( Peyré and Cuturi, 2019 ) . The semi-discrete nature of the problem allows us to characterize precisely the structure of the transport.

sections.heading: Appendix B Related Work
sections.text: Accelerated parallel sampling for language models broadly spans three paradigms: (i) distilling and accelerating multi-step discrete diffusion models ( Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2025 ; Hayakawa et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Israel et al., 2025 ) ; (ii) continuous-space generative modeling, which embeds categorical tokens into continuous Euclidean or spherical geometries ( Li et al., 2022 ; Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026 ; Yoo et al., 2026 ) ; (iii) parallelizing AR models ( Kou et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026b ) . Diffusion or flow matching models can be integrated into few-step samplers via flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025 ) . Extending diffusion and flow maps to discrete categorical representations and language models ( Eijkelboom et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Roos et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026a ) embeds tokens into continuous spaces. Nonetheless, these models universally rely on independent couplings p ⁡ ( x 0 , x 1 ) = p ⁡ ( x 0 ) ​ p ​ ( x 1 ) p(x_{0},x_{1})=p(x_{0})p(x_{1}) , causing straight paths connecting random pairs to cross in high dimensions and forcing the velocity field to curve. Rectified Flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) showed that straighter trajectories permit better generation with coarse numerical integration. The key distinction between GSF and these methods is the use of teacher-guided noise-data pairs as pioneered by, e.g. ( Draxler et al., 2026 ) . Gumbel Distillation ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) directly utilizes Gumbels sampled from an AR teacher’s posterior distribution to supervise a student model. However, Gumbel Distillation binds this pairing to a discrete diffusion backbone, which requires iterative categorical transitions and multiple sampling steps. GSF sits at the intersection of continuous flow matching and AR distillation. Standard Rectified Flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) can iteratively apply computationally expensive Reflow steps to obtain increasingly straight paths. It uses this insight as a strong inductive bias for learning the noise-data pairing using existing flow map techniques.

sections.heading: Why use a flow map?
sections.text: If the student model were trained to perfection, it would only need to learn a direct mapping from the initial noise 𝝃 {\bm{\xi}} to the data 𝐱 1 {\mathbf{x}}_{1} . Indeed, we find that directly learning this mapping yields higher token accuracy than a flow map parameterization. For example, in unconditional generation on OpenWebText, the direct one-step model achieves an accuracy of 9.92 % 9.92\% , whereas our flow-map-based GSF achieves 6.68 % 6.68\% . However, this accuracy remains too low to produce coherent text, resulting in poor generation quality with a GM score exceeding 30 30 . This indicates that relying solely on deterministic pairing is insufficient for faithful generation. Therefore, motivated by the strong generative performance of flow maps, we instead focus on enhancing generative quality by discovering straight trajectories and utilizing them within the flow map framework.

sections.heading: Performance gap.
sections.text: Another clear limitation of our method is the remaining performance gap compared to the AR teacher. In the image domain, learning a flow map along a given trajectory often yields performance comparable to that of the teacher ( Song et al., 2023 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) , making such a pronounced gap unexpected. We suspect that the high dimensionality of L × | 𝒱 | L\times|{\mathcal{V}}| is the primary cause. Furthermore, unlike pixel space, which is relatively robust to minor deviations, prediction errors in one-hot space can abruptly produce entirely different tokens. Another concurrent work, D-MMD ( Hoogeboom et al., 2026 ) , achieves better results than GSF at NFE = 4 \text{NFE}=4 (Table 9 ). D-MMD uses distribution matching with an auxiliary network, a paradigm that can outperform trajectory-based methods even in image generation ( Salimans et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2024 ) . However, the auxiliary network introduces substantial memory and computational overhead and can make training less stable; thus, the two approaches are not directly comparable. In particular, D-MMD uses 318.1M parameters, nearly twice the size of GSF (167.8M). For completeness, we report our D-MMD results in Table 9 . Since D-MMD lacks inherent deterministic noise-data pairing, it did not produce meaningful results at one- or two-step sampling. We theoretically demonstrate that the coupling between Gumbel noise and one-hot token sequences induced by an autoregressive model yields non-intersecting linear paths connecting the noise to the sequence representations. To further enhance high-quality few-step path sampling, we use a flow map semigroup objective where the tangent (velocity) condition is guided directly by the AR teacher. Across various benchmarks, including pretraining and downstream tasks, GSF can outperform current few-step language generation baselines. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Efficiency-performance trade-offs for GSF, primary distillation baselines (varying step sizes), and AR models (varying model sizes). Model Parallel Generation Deterministic Pairing Straight Path Autoregressive Model ✗ ✓ ✓ Discrete Diffusion Model ✓ ✗ ✗ Continuous Flow (Diffusion) ✓ ✓ ✗ Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF) ✓ ✓ ✓ Autoregressive models (AR) are widely used for language generation due to their strong generative performance. However, their sequential generation process is computationally expensive. To address this limitation, parallel-generation language models based on discrete diffusion or continuous flow models have been introduced ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026a ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, discrete diffusion and continuous-flow models often require many sampling steps to control factorization or discretization errors. To accelerate inference in parallel generative models, a natural direction is distillation, i.e., compressing multi-step iterative generation into a few sampling steps or a single step ( Song et al., 2023 ; Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2025 ; Hayakawa et al., 2025 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2026 ) , often using a discrete diffusion model as a teacher. Given their better empirical performance on text modeling, we explore whether autoregressive (AR) models can be used as more capable teachers. Recent work harnesses AR teachers to supervise parallel student models by constructing deterministic sequence-level noise–data pairs ( Draxler et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . However, learning sequence-level noise-to-data mappings is an exceptionally hard supervised problem; for instance, Gumbel-Distill (GD) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) must still fall back to multi-step refinement over a discrete diffusion backbone. In this paper, we instead define a flow path in one-hot continuous space directly over the AR model’s Gumbel-max sampling. This defines a coupling between the distribution of Gumbel sequences 𝐱 0 {\mathbf{x}}_{0} and corresponding one-hot token vectors 𝐱 1 {\mathbf{x}}_{1} such that, for endpoints distributed according to this coupling, the linear interpolants 𝐱 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝐱 0 + t ​ 𝐱 1 {\mathbf{x}}_{t}=(1-t){\mathbf{x}}_{0}+t{\mathbf{x}}_{1} do not intersect ( Figure 2 ). Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF) then learns these straight paths provided by an AR teacher while enabling parallel generation. Straight paths are desirable: minimizing trajectory curvature allows numerical ODE solvers to generate samples in a few steps without discretization issues ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . We further enhance few-step performance using a flow map parameterization (FMLM) ( Lee et al., 2026 ) where the straight tangent (velocity) supervision is given by the AR teacher. Few-step distillation performance on OpenWebText. Next, we evaluate few-step sampling using the flow map objective across 1, 2, and 4 sampling steps ( Table 4 ). At NFE = 1 \text{NFE}=1 , GSF achieves 114.9 generative perplexity and a gradient moment score of 0.94, outperforming prior distillation models in this step regime. Whereas discrete diffusion distillation baselines collapse at single-step sampling (SDTT: 1260.8; DCD: 5743.2; Di4C (Duo): 370.5), GSF preserves reasonable performance. We also maintain an edge over FMLM variants (FMLM: 168.3; FMLM-re: 140.0). However, GD uses a discrete diffusion backbone and does not explicitly exploit path information, resulting in limited performance (PPL: 1475.9) compared with GSF. This may be because directly learning the mapping from Gumbel noise to data is an extremely difficult supervised problem. In contrast, the continuous straight path can provide useful intermediate supervision that helps the model learn this mapping more effectively. We investigate the impact of prior choice and time reparameterization for single-step generation on OpenWebText ( Table 8 ). Using the raw Standard Gumbel prior yields poor gradient moment score ( GM = 1.76 \text{GM}=1.76 , PPL = 133.5 \text{PPL}=133.5 ), which we hypothesize is due to the strong right skew of extreme-value distributions ( Figure 4(a) ). Transforming the prior to a standard Gaussian via Proposition 2 substantially improves GM ( GM = 1.05 \text{GM}=1.05 under linear scheduling). Next, we compare noise schedules: while standard DER parameterization achieves 113.8 PPL, it incurs a higher GM score (1.26) and lower token entropy (4.84). Our Coupled DER schedule ( Figure 4(b) ) obtains the best overall balance: GM = 0.94 \text{GM}=0.94 , PPL = 114.9 \text{PPL}=114.9 , and Ent = 5.07 \text{Ent}=5.07 . Training and architectural configurations. Table 8 examines the impact of student architecture and training configurations for 1-step generation on OpenWebText: (i) Attention masking : Replacing bidirectional self-attention with causal masking drastically degrades performance ( PPL = 211.0 \text{PPL}=211.0 , GM = 1.62 \text{GM}=1.62 ). While the causal dependencies are enough to model straight trajectories defined by the autoregressive teacher, parallel non-autoregressive generation benefits from bidirectional context: the teacher’s Gumbel coupling provides sequence-level target supervision, but bidirectional self-attention enables the student to coordinate across all tokens simultaneously. (ii) Teacher weight initialization : Training a randomly initialized student increases perplexity from 114.9 to 145.4, showing that transferring pretrained AR teacher representations provides an effective initialization for flow map distillation.
